unit.title: Can Machines Be Creative?
objectives: I can compare two viewpoints in an argument.
I can evaluate which evidence supports a claim.
I can write an argument that responds to an opposing view.

paragraphs: When an image generated by artificial intelligence won first prize in the digital art category of a state fair competition in the United States in 2022, many artists were furious. The winner had typed a series of instructions into a program, adjusted the results, and submitted the final picture. To some observers, this was simply a new kind of tool; to others, it was a threat to the very definition of art.

Those who defend AI-generated work point out that every major technology has provoked similar fears. When photography appeared in the nineteenth century, some painters worried that their craft would become obsolete. Instead, photography developed into an art form of its own, and painting moved in new, more experimental directions. From this perspective, AI may augment human creativity rather than replace it.

Critics, however, argue that the comparison is misleading. A photographer still chooses the subject, the light, and the moment, whereas an AI system produces images by recombining patterns learned from millions of existing works, often without the original creators' permission. If creativity requires intention and personal experience, they ask, can a system that has neither be called creative at all?

The debate is unlikely to be settled soon, but it is forcing society to reconsider questions that once seemed purely philosophical. Who deserves credit for a work produced by a human and a machine together? Should artists be paid when their styles are used to train software? How we answer may shape not only the future of art, but also how we value human imagination itself.

In 2022, a picture made with artificial intelligence (AI) won first prize at an art contest in the United States. The winner typed instructions into a computer program, changed the results, and sent in the final picture. Some people said AI is just a new tool. Others were angry. They felt it was a danger to real art.

People who defend AI art say new technology always makes people afraid at first. When cameras were invented, some painters worried that their skill would become obsolete, or no longer needed. But photography became a new kind of art, and painters tried new styles. So AI may augment, or add to, human creativity instead of replacing it.

Critics say this comparison is not fair. A photographer still chooses what to shoot, the light, and the right moment. But AI makes pictures by mixing patterns from millions of old artworks, often without asking the artists. If being creative needs a clear goal and real life experience, can a machine without them be creative?

People will not agree soon. But this debate makes us ask new questions. Who should get credit when a person and a machine make art together? Should artists get money when their styles are used to train computers? Our answers may change how we see art and human imagination.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?

options.text: How to win an art competition with AI
options.feedback: The contest is only the opening example.

options.text: The debate over whether AI-generated work counts as creative art
The history of photography in the nineteenth century
options.feedback: Photography is used as a comparison in one paragraph.

options.text: Why artists should stop using computers
options.feedback: The writer does not give this advice.

questions.explanation: The passage presents defenders (P2) and critics (P3) and ends with open questions (P4) — a debate about AI and creativity.

hints.text: Compare the first sentences of paragraphs 2 and 3.
Key words: "Those who defend" vs. "Critics, however".
Options A and C are details used as examples.
Two sides + open questions = a debate. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Why do defenders of AI art mention the history of photography?

options.text: To suggest that fears about new technology can turn out to be wrong
To prove that photographers are better artists than painters
options.feedback: The paragraph does not rank artists.

options.text: To argue that painting has disappeared
options.feedback: Painting moved in new directions — it did not disappear.

questions.explanation: Painters feared photography, but both art forms survived. Defenders use this analogy to argue AI fears may also be unfounded.

hints.text: In paragraph 2, what did painters fear? What actually happened?
Key words: "worried" → "Instead".
Option C contradicts the text.
This is an analogy: past fear → good outcome, so the present fear may be wrong too. Answer: A.

questions.stem: According to the critics, how is AI different from photography?

options.text: AI is more expensive than a camera.
A photographer makes personal choices, while AI recombines existing works.
Photography requires no skill at all.
options.feedback: The critics say the photographer chooses subject, light, and moment — that is skill.

questions.explanation: "A photographer still chooses ... whereas an AI system produces images by recombining patterns." whereas 表對比。

hints.text: Find the word "whereas" in paragraph 3. It shows a contrast.
Compare: "chooses the subject, the light, and the moment" vs. "recombining patterns".
Option A is not mentioned.
Human choice vs. machine recombination. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence would most strengthen the critics' argument?

options.text: A study showing that many AI systems were trained on artworks without the artists' permission
A report that cameras became cheaper in the 1900s
options.feedback: Camera prices do not relate to the critics' point about intention or permission.

options.text: A survey showing that most people enjoy looking at AI images
options.feedback: Enjoyment does not prove anything about creativity or permission — and might help the defenders.

questions.explanation: The critics argue AI recombines others' work "often without the original creators' permission". Evidence of unauthorized training directly supports that claim.

hints.text: First, list the critics' two main points in paragraph 3.
Critics' points: (1) without permission (2) no intention or experience. Which option matches one of them?
Option B is unrelated to the critics' claims.
Good evidence must connect directly to the claim. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Smartphones have made many paper maps nearly ___; few people buy them anymore.

options.feedback: Essential means "necessary" — but few people buy them.

hints.text: The part after ";" explains the blank.
You need a word meaning "no longer used".
Option C describes people's feelings.
Answer: obsolete.

questions.stem: Teachers can use AI tools to ___ their lessons, not to replace their own teaching.

options.feedback: Abandon means "give up" — the opposite of "not replace".

questions.explanation: augment = add to / make stronger（增強）; "not to replace" signals adding, not removing.

hints.text: Look at "not to replace". The blank is the opposite idea.
You need a word meaning "add to / make stronger".
Option C means to give up.
Answer: augment.

questions.stem: Can AI be truly creative? Write an argument that states your position, gives two reasons, and responds to one opposing view.

frames: In my view, AI ___ truly creative.
scaffolds.model_text: In my view, AI is not truly creative, although it is a powerful creative tool. To begin with, creativity requires intention. A human artist decides what feeling or idea to express, while an AI system only follows patterns in its training data. Moreover, many AI systems learn from artworks without the creators' permission, so their results depend on other people's originality. Some people argue that photography was also once called a threat to art. However, a photographer still makes personal choices about the subject and the moment, which AI cannot do on its own. Ultimately, AI can augment human creativity, but the creative spark still comes from people.
checklist: I gave two reasons with support.
I described an opposing view fairly.
I responded to the opposing view.

questions.explanation: A strong argument acknowledges the other side and explains why your position is still more convincing.

hints.text: Decide your position, then reread paragraphs 2 and 3 to find one idea from each side.
Structure: Position → Reason 1 → Reason 2 → Counterclaim → Rebuttal → Conclusion.
Sample counterclaim + rebuttal: "Some people argue that AI is just a new tool. However, ..."
Read the model argument, then write your own.
